parts: Policy: Security is seen as an IT-only responsibility. There are no formal, documented policies or standards for data security.
Roles & Responsibilities: There is no designated "Data Security Owner." Data professionals are generally unaware of their security responsibilities.
Compliance: Compliance with regulations (e.g., GDPR, HIPAA) is not systematically addressed.
Policy: Basic data security policies are drafted but may not be widely communicated or enforced. They often focus on high-level statements rather than specific technical controls.

Roles & Responsibilities: Basic security roles are defined (e.g., data owners are identified), but accountability is not consistently enforced. Some data professionals are given basic security training.
Compliance: An initial gap analysis against key regulations (e.g., GDPR, HIPAA) is performed, but remediation efforts are still project-based and reactive.
Data Classification: Data is not formally classified. Data engineers may have a vague idea of sensitive data but rely on tribal knowledge.
Access Control: Access to data is managed on an as-needed basis. Users are often granted broad permissions (e.g., `READ-ALL`) to simplify their work.
Data Protection: Encryption is handled by the platform by default, but there is no custom configuration.
Data Masking/Anonymization: No systematic data masking is in place. Data is used in its raw form in development or test environments.
Network Security: Data platforms are accessed directly over the public internet. There's no use of private endpoints or firewalls to restrict network access.
Data Classification: Some data is manually classified, often just into two or three categories (e.g., public, confidential, PII). This process is inconsistent and relies on manual effort.

Access Control: A policy of least privilege is discussed but not yet fully implemented. Access to production data is restricted to a small group, but development environments still use overly permissive roles.
Data Protection: Data is encrypted at rest and in transit using the platform's default capabilities. Some key concepts around customer-managed keys (CMK) are being explored but not implemented.
Data Masking/Anonymization: Basic, ad-hoc data masking is performed for some sensitive fields in non-production environments, but there is no consistent, automated process.
Network Security: Network access is limited to a whitelist of IP addresses. Basic network policies are in place to control access to specific platforms.
Logging & Auditing: Logging is enabled by default, but logs are not regularly reviewed or analyzed for suspicious activity. They are only used after an incident occurs.
Incident Response: There is no formal data security incident response plan. In the event of a breach, response is ad-hoc and chaotic.
Logging & Auditing: Basic logging and auditing are enabled. A central log collection system is being set up, but logs are not yet correlated or analyzed for behavioral anomalies.
Incident Response: A basic incident response plan is drafted, but it is not regularly tested or practiced. Roles are defined but not well-understood by all stakeholders.
Code Security: There is no formal process for securing data pipeline code. Secrets and credentials may be hardcoded or stored in insecure locations.
Secure Design: Security is not considered during the design phase of data pipelines. The focus is on functionality and performance, not security.
Code Security: Basic checks are performed on code for hardcoded secrets, often manually. Secrets management is being introduced, but it's not yet integrated into the development workflow.
Secure Design: Security is considered a non-functional requirement. Basic threat modeling is performed for critical data pipelines.
Deployment Process: Data pipelines are deployed manually with no security checks or controls. The same pipeline is often used for both production and non-production environments.
Deployment Process: A basic CI/CD pipeline is in use, but security checks are not integrated. Manual approval steps are in place, but they don't include security reviews.
Training: There is no formal data security training for data professionals. Security is only discussed after an incident.
Training: Basic, ad-hoc security training is provided to data professionals, often through informal channels like a single presentation. There is no consistent curriculum or ongoing education.
Security Testing: There is no formal security testing of data pipelines or platforms. Security is assumed to be handled by the platform.
Security Testing: Basic security testing is performed, but it's often a manual, one-off effort (e.g., a simple vulnerability scan on a data pipeline). It is not part of a regular testing cycle.
